fixes.explanation: Suppress is the word. Paul, the apostle (Romans 1:1) writing this letter to believers in Rome (Romans 1:7), says these are men "…who suppress the truth by their wickedness." You know that move where you hold a beach ball underwater? It takes effort, and it keeps wanting to pop right back up. The truth is right there, and they're sitting on it.

Workmanship is right. Paul says God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, are "…understood from His workmanship…" His qualities are invisible, but what He made can be seen. It's like how you can tell a lot about a cook from one look at the cookie tray.

Messengers makes sense, since God does send people with words (Hebrews 1:1), and I've met an angel myself. But this verse doesn't mention any messengers. Paul says God's invisible qualities are "…understood from His workmanship…" The evidence is what He made.

Without excuse is exactly what Paul says. God's invisible qualities "…have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse." Clearly seen leaves very little room for "I had no idea." It's like telling the boss you had no idea the report was due when it's been on your calendar in red.

It's an easy thing to assume, but Paul says the opposite. He writes, "For although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him…" They knew Him. Knowing Him didn't mean they glorified Him as God or gave thanks.
Gold and silver is a common thing to trade for, but it's not in this verse. Paul says they exchanged God's glory "…for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles." It's a strange list.

That's what the text says: "Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another." This is a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be. Notice the words: God gave them over.

A flood did happen in the Bible, in Noah's day (Genesis 6:17). Noah, by the way, was the man God told to build an ark (Genesis 6:14). But that's a different passage. Here the text says, "…God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity…"

Creature is the word. Paul says they "…worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator…" Those two words look a lot alike, but there's one big difference. It's like swapping the person who baked your cookies for the cookie.

Law is a reasonable guess, since Paul writes about it elsewhere in this letter (Romans 3:20). But here he says they "…worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator…" The contrast is between what was made and the One who made it.

A time of testing sounds like a sensible next step, and the Bible does talk about testing in other places (James 1:12). But in this verse Paul says, "…He gave them up to a depraved mind…" Nothing in it says anything about a test.
True. Paul says God gave them up to a depraved mind, "…to do what ought not to be done." That's just what the verse says. The depraved mind and the doing sit in the same sentence.

That's it. Paul says, "…they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them." Knowing the decree didn't stop them. They kept going and approved of those who practice these things, which is a hard thing to read.
